Mandatory Access Control (MAC) is a prison: even the warden needs a signed policy to open a cell. Security: Security field guide · defensive framing How hacking actually happens. Films show a hooded figure, a green terminal, and fifteen seconds of typing that opens a bank. Reality is duller and far more effective: an unlocked door, a stolen password, an unpatched server nobody remembered was facing the internet. This guide walks the eight levels of real intrusion technique, with a documented case file, a code sample and the defense that would have stopped it at each one. 8 levels of technique Documented case files Mapped to MITRE ATT&CK Every claim sourced ~60% of breaches involved a human element (Verizon DBIR 2025) 44% of breaches involved ransomware, up 37% year over year (DBIR 2025) 30% of breaches involved a third party — double the prior year (DBIR 2025) 20% used exploitation of a vulnerability to get in, +34% YoY (DBIR 2025) $115k median ransom actually paid; 64% of victims refused to pay (DBIR 2025) Reality vs. the movies Start here Real intrusions are not spells. They are a sequence of unremarkable steps, each one cheap, each one avoidable. The industry has a shared vocabulary for those steps — MITRE ATT&CK, which currently catalogues 15 tactics, 227 techniques and 479 sub-techniques for enterprise environments alone [1] [2] . This page follows that shape, level by level. Myth: hackers break cryptography Modern encryption is not the weak point. They log in with someone's valid password instead. Reality Valid accounts and stolen credentials recur in nearly every case below. In the 2024 Snowflake intrusions, every incident investigated traced back to compromised customer credentials [37] . Myth: it takes a genius Attack tooling is commoditised, sold as a subscription, and often operated by people who understand the business poorly and the tooling not at all. Reality The MGM Resorts intrusion was not won with an exploit. It was won by persuading a help desk to reset a password [19] . The victim's filing put the impact at roughly $100 million [18] . Myth: zero-days are required Zero-days are expensive, perishable ammunition. Most intrusions use a vulnerability the vendor patched months ago — or no vulnerability at all. Reality Change Healthcare in 2024 was not a novel attack: a system simply wasn't using multifactor authentication [20] . Myth: it's over in seconds Dwell time is long. SUNBURST, the SolarWinds backdoor, deliberately waited roughly two weeks before even phoning home. Reality Detection rarely fails because the attacker was fast. It fails because nobody was looking at the logs that already said what happened. The ladder, at a glance Levels 0–4 are about getting in . Levels 5–6 are about staying in and getting around . Levels 7–8 are about what the access is worth . An attacker rarely needs all eight — most intrusions end at level 2 or 3 and still work. Level What it really means ATT&CK anchor Cost to attacker 0 · Recon Read what the target published: services, staff, secrets, software versions TA0043 Near zero 1 · Default creds Log in to a device still using the factory password T1078, T1110 Near zero 2 · Reuse Try passwords stolen from other breaches against this one T1110.004 Very low 3 · Social engineering Persuade a person to hand over access or approve a prompt T1566, T1078 Low, scales 4 · Exploit a service Abuse a software flaw in something reachable from the internet T1190 Low to high 5 · Escalate & move Turn one foothold into domain-wide control, quietly T1003, T1550.002 Moderate 6 · Persist & exfiltrate Beacon home on a schedule, blend with normal traffic, take the data T1071, T1219 Moderate 7 · Impact Encrypt, leak, sell, extort or commit fraud TA0040 Low once inside 8 · Nation-state Supply-chain code, purpose-built zero-days, air-gap crossing T1195, T1190 Very high Read the ladder as a budget. Every rung is a trade: sophistication costs money and risks attention; an unlocked door costs nothing and often works. That is why the boring rungs — 1, 2 and 3 — carry most of the real intrusions, and why the exotic rung 8 gets the headlines. Level 0 · Reconnaissance 0 Seeing what you left facing the internet MITRE ATT&CK TA0043 Reconnaissance · “Hacking” begins with reading, not breaking. Before anything is attacked, it is measured. Public-facing IP ranges are scanned continuously and indexed: which hosts, which ports, which software versions. Subdomains leak in certificate transparency logs. Job adverts name the exact products a company runs. Source-code repositories leak far more than code — sometimes live credentials. None of this is illegal in most jurisdictions, and all of it is automated. The attacker's real question at this level is simple: what is exposed, and who can log into it? Case file Uber, 2016 — the key that was sitting in Git The access chain behind Uber's 2016 breach is a perfect illustration of levels 0, 2 and 3 stacked together. According to the US Federal Trade Commission, an engineer had placed an AWS access key in plain text inside a private GitHub repository , and the intruders reached those repositories using engineer passwords exposed in other large data breaches — Uber did not require MFA for repository access and did not prohibit password reuse [25] . The FTC's figures: over one month, intruders downloaded 25.6 million names and email addresses , 22.1 million names and mobile numbers , and 607,000 driver's-licence numbers [25] . California's Attorney General described the exposure as data of 57 million users ; Uber later settled nationwide for $148 million over the breach and the delayed disclosure [26] . Two mundane controls — mandatory MFA on the code host, and never storing long-lived keys in a repository — would each have broken the chain. secret-hunt — what a repo leak looks like from outside bash # One command over a repo's entire history, including deleted files. # (These two values are AWS's own public documentation examples.) $ git log -p --all | grep -nE 'AKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}' +aws_access_key_id = AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE +aws_secret_access_key = wJalrXUtnFEMI/K7MDENG/bPxRfiCYEXAMPLEKEY # Deleted commits are not deleted. History is the leak surface. $ git log --all --oneline -- .env 4f9a1c2 rotate keys a03bb77 initial commit <-- the secret still lives here the fix — remove the long-lived key entirely ini # ~/.aws/config — no stored secret to steal in the first place. [default] region = us-east-1 credential_process = aws-sso-credential-process # Or, in CI, an OIDC workload identity that mints short-lived # credentials per job. Nothing long-lived to leak, nothing to rotate. Why “private repository” is not a security control A private repo is an authorisation decision made by one vendor, protecting a secret you do not control, sitting behind a password that a human chose and may reuse. It is one factor. Once an attacker holds a valid engineer session — as in the Uber case — private and public look identical. Treat every repository as eventually public and every key as eventually leaked: that is why short-lived, scoped credentials beat long-lived ones regardless of where they live. What stops it Secret scanning in the pipeline , plus history scanning — catch the key before a human forgets it. No long-lived cloud keys. Use SSO, OIDC and workload identity so there is nothing durable to steal. Cut your internet surface. Inventory what is actually reachable; kill forgotten endpoints and test environments. Mandatory MFA on the code host — this alone broke the Uber chain at the first step. Level 1 · The unlocked front door 1 Devices still using the factory password MITRE ATT&CK T1078 Valid Accounts · T1110 Brute Force · Default and weak credentials The cheapest possible intrusion: a device that ships with admin/admin , is never changed, and is reachable from the internet on an administrative port. No exploit, no cleverness — just a login form left as the vendor designed it. Case file Mirai, 2016 — 62 default passwords, one botnet Mirai scanned the internet continuously for internet-of-things devices — routers, cameras, DVRs — and logged in with a list of 62 common default usernames and passwords . Each compromised device joined a botnet used for distributed denial-of-service attacks. CISA advised network defenders to watch Telnet ports 23 and 2323 for unauthorised access attempts [29] . CISA attributed a DDoS exceeding 620 Gbps against KrebsOnSecurity to Mirai, and a separate Mirai attack on OVH of at least 1.1 Tbps [29] . CISA cited the Mirai author's claim of more than 380,000 IoT devices enlisted for the Krebs attack [29] . Mirai was also associated with the October 2016 Dyn DNS outage, which made major sites briefly unreachable for many users; the SEI's write-up describes Mirai's role cautiously, as one factor among several [30] . No CVE was needed for the original mechanism. The weakness was a known default credential on an exposed port. /var/log/auth.log — the shape of the attack, from the defender's side text $ grep -E 'Failed password|Invalid user' /var/log/auth.log | tail -6 Oct 16 03:14:02 host sshd[2919]: Invalid user admin from 185.203.16.77 port 51422 Oct 16 03:14:03 host sshd[2921]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 185.203.16.77 port 51438 Oct 16 03:14:04 host sshd[2923]: Invalid user root from 185.203.16.77 port 51451 Oct 16 03:14:05 host sshd[2925]: Failed password for invalid user root from 185.203.16.77 port 51466 Oct 16 03:14:06 host sshd[2927]: Invalid user pi from 185.203.16.77 port 51479 Oct 16 03:14:07 host sshd[2929]: Failed password for invalid user pi from 185.203.16.77 port 51491 # Rank sources by failed-auth volume. (Field position varies with the # message shape, so pin it with a named-pattern parser in production.) $ grep 'Failed password' /var/log/auth.log \ | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3 4182 185.203.16.77 <-- block this source and investigate 91 91.240.118.4 12 172.16.4.19 <-- internal, wrong password: talk to that user the fix — make the default impossible and unreachable jsonc // The remedy is deliberately boring, which is why it gets skipped. { "device" : "camera-fw-4.2" , "change_on_first_boot" : [ "admin" ], // enforced at setup, not suggested "telnet" : { "enabled" : false }, // the port Mirai needed "mgmt_interface" : "vlan-99" , // reachable from the mgmt network only "egress_policy" : "deny-by-default" // a compromised camera cannot call out } What stops it Change defaults at onboarding , on a process that fails closed if the step is skipped. Turn off what you don't use: Telnet, UPnP, vendor cloud bridges, debug ports. Segment the device class. Cameras and printers should not reach the finance VLAN or the internet freely. Rate-limit and alert on authentication failures per source, and block or tarpit on threshold. Inventory the unowned. Most default-credential casualties are devices no one knows they own. Level 2 · Password reuse & credential stuffing 2 Your password was valid here because it was valid somewhere else MITRE ATT&CK T1110.004 Credential Stuffing · T1078 Valid Accounts · T1555 Credentials from Password Stores Credential stuffing takes username/password pairs leaked from one service and tries them on another, exploiting the fact that people reuse passwords. MITRE describes the technique as gaining access through “ credential overlap ” — users reusing passwords across personal and business accounts [36] . Add infostealer malware, which harvests saved credentials and session data from a victim's own machine and uploads them to a marketplace, and the attacker never needs to break anything at all. They are simply logging in as an employee. Case file The 2024 Snowflake campaign — AT&T, Ticketmaster, Santander This is the reference example of level 2 at scale. Mandiant tracked the financially motivated actor as UNC5537 and reported that every incident it investigated was traced back to compromised customer credentials , with no evidence the activity came from a breach of Snowflake's own environment. The credentials had previously been stolen by infostealer malware on systems that were not Snowflake's; at least 79.7% of the accounts the actor used had prior credential exposure. In the incidents analysed, MFA was not enabled, valid credentials had sometimes gone unrotated for years, and network allow lists were absent. Mandiant and Snowflake had notified approximately 165 potentially exposed organisations [37] . AT&T told the SEC that an attacker accessed a workspace on a third-party cloud platform and exfiltrated files between April 14 and April 25, 2024 . The data covered call and text-interaction records for roughly May–October 2022 and one day in January 2023, and the filing says it covered “nearly all of AT&T's wireless customers.” The filing itself does not state a numeric total [38] . The widely reported figure of roughly 109 million US customer accounts comes from contemporaneous reporting and describes accounts, not individual call records [39] [40] . Ticketmaster confirmed “unauthorized activity on an isolated cloud database hosted by a third-party data services provider” and did not name the provider or confirm the frequently repeated 560-million figure [41] . Santander confirmed unauthorised access to a third-party-hosted database affecting certain customers in Chile, Spain and Uruguay, while stating that no credentials allowing transactions were contained in that database [42] . Case file 23andMe, 2023 — 14,000 logins, 6.9 million profiles A useful lesson in reading breach numbers carefully. 23andMe said an actor accessed a select number of individual accounts using credential stuffing — credentials reused from other compromised websites . The confirmed figure was roughly 14,000 accounts , under 0.1% of its customers. Through those accounts, the actor reached approximately 5.5 million DNA Relatives profiles and 1.4 million Family Tree profiles — about 6.9 million profiles in total , which is not the same as 6.9 million compromised logins [43] . Fourteen thousand reused passwords produced a headline about nearly seven million people: the blast radius of one login is every other account it can see . Vendor measurement of the underlying behaviour: SpyCloud reported a 74% reuse rate among users exposed in two or more breaches during the prior year, and a 61% historical reuse rate for previously exposed passwords through 2023. These describe SpyCloud's analysed exposure population, not a survey of all internet users [44] [45] . login.py — the version that feeds credential stuffing python # ✖ Fast hash, no rate limit, verbose errors, no MFA gate. import hashlib def login (db, email, password): row = db.execute( "SELECT pw_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?" , (email,) ).fetchone() if row is None : return "No account with that email" # enumeration: tells the attacker who exists if row[ "pw_hash" ] == hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest(): return "ok" # MD5: billions of guesses per second on a GPU return "Wrong password" # and nothing limits how often this runs login.py — hardened for exactly this attack python # ✓ Memory-hard hash, per-source throttle, uniform responses, MFA continuation. from argon2 import PasswordHasher from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError ph = PasswordHasher() def login (db, cache, email, password, ip, device): # 1. Throttle by source *and* by account: stuffing sprays one account # across thousands of IPs, and thousands of accounts from one IP. for key in ( f"rl:ip:{ip}" , f"rl:acct:{email}" ): if cache.incr(key) == 1 : cache.expire(key, 900 ) if int (cache.get(key) or 0 ) > 10 : return generic_failure () # same shape as a wrong password row = db.execute( "SELECT id, pw_hash, totp_secret FROM users WHERE email = ?" , (email,) ).fetchone() try : if row and ph.verify(row[ "pw_hash" ], password): if ph.check_needs_rehash(row[ "pw_hash" ]): db.execute( "UPDATE users SET pw_hash = ? WHERE id = ?" , (ph.hash(password), row[ "id" ])) return require_mfa (row[ "id" ], device) # password alone is not a session except VerifyMismatchError: pass return generic_failure () # no enumeration, no detail, no oracle The MFA line is the whole defense. In the Snowflake campaign, credentials were valid but MFA was simply not enabled, and in some cases the same credential had gone unrotated for years [37] . A stolen password plus a second factor the attacker does not have is just a failed login. What stops it MFA everywhere, then make it phishing-resistant (see level 3) — this defeats stolen passwords outright. Argon2id or bcrypt for storage, so a stolen hash is not a cheap offline crack. Screen passwords against breach corpora at set-password and login time — a reused password is a known password. Throttle per account and per IP , with uniform error messages to avoid account enumeration. Rotate and scope service credentials , and set network allow lists where the vendor supports them. Assume endpoint compromise. Infostealers make credential theft trivial; endpoint hardening is a credential control too. Level 3 · Social engineering 3 Hacking the people who legitimately have access MITRE ATT&CK T1566 Phishing · T1078 Valid Accounts · MFA fatigue / help-desk impersonation Social engineering is not a lesser form of hacking; it is the highest-yield one, because it targets the component that is hardest to patch and most willing to be helpful. Three variants dominate real incidents: Phishing — a message that convinces a person to enter credentials on a page the attacker controls, or to open an attachment. MFA fatigue / push bombing — the attacker already holds the password and repeatedly triggers push prompts until the victim approves one out of irritation or confusion. Help-desk impersonation — the attacker calls the service desk as an employee, and asks them to reset the password or enrol a new authenticator. Case file MGM Resorts, 2023 — a help desk, not an exploit Public reporting attributes the intrusion to the Scattered Spider group using help-desk social engineering. CISA's advisory on the group describes precisely this tactic: persuading help-desk staff to reset passwords or reissue MFA tokens. MGM's own SEC filing does not state the initial-access method or name the actors, so the specific reported impersonation sequence is press attribution rather than a company confirmation [18] [19] . MGM estimated a negative impact of approximately $100 million to Adjusted Property EBITDAR and reported less than $10 million in one-time expenses at that point [18] . The filing says personal information was obtained for some customers who had transacted before March 2019 , and that bank-account and payment-card information were not obtained [18] . No CVE. Nothing was exploited — the account-recovery process was. Case file Target, 2013 — a contractor's credentials, and 40 million cards Attackers entered Target's network using network credentials stolen from Fazio Mechanical Services , Target's HVAC and refrigeration contractor. They then placed card-stealing malware on point-of-sale systems and moved the stolen data out to external drop servers. Reporting attributes the credential theft to a malware-bearing phishing email; the readable account confirms the stolen vendor credentials as the entry, and establishes phishing less firmly [21] [22] . Approximately 40 million debit and credit card accounts were exposed [21] . Target's 2015 filing is reported to show $252 million in cumulative breach expenses, offset by $90 million of insurance, for a net $162 million [23] . The control failure was not a missing patch. Snort: Home Snort 3 / Operator Signature engine · Snort 3, DAQ, inline drop Snort 3: the sensor you can explain line by line Snort 3 replaced a C configuration file with Lua, replaced the old preprocessor maze with a modular pipeline and kept the one thing that matters: a signature language simple enough to read at three in the morning. This manual covers the build, the config, DAQ capture, rule anatomy, inline blocking and the hardening that keeps a sensor from becoming another attack surface. snort.lua afpacket + NFQUEUE inline IPS systemd caps 01 One engine, three postures Snort is usually described as an IDS, which undersells the same code running three ways. The posture decides where packets enter, whether Snort can drop them, and what a failure means. Posture Packet path Can drop Use it for IDS Copy of traffic on a tap or SPAN No Detection, visibility, tuning rules without consequences IPS Traffic flows through Snort Yes, in inline mode Enforcing a small, well-tested rule set Offline Reading a pcap file No Proving a rule fires before you trust it in line Snort 2 and Snort 3 are different products with a shared name and rule syntax: the config file changed language, the plugin interface changed, and some rule options were replaced. Check which one you have before copying any tutorial. snort -V # ,,_ -*> Snort! <*- # o" )~ Version 3.1.x ... snort --help | head -20 snort --list-modules | head # modules differ per build 02 Build it (and verify the build) Distro packages exist, but they are often Snort 2.x with a different config layout. On Debian the honest route for Snort 3 is a source build against the current DAQ library, installed under /usr/local so the version is unambiguous. sudo apt install -y build-essential libpcap-dev libpcre2-dev libdumbnet-dev \ bison flex liblzma-dev zlib1g-dev libssl-dev libhwloc-dev libluajit-5.1-dev \ pkg-config cmake git # DAQ first: Snort 3 needs a matching libdaq git clone https://github.com/snort3/libdaq.git && cd libdaq ./bootstrap && ./configure && make -j"$(nproc)" && sudo make install && sudo ldconfig # then Snort itself git clone https://github.com/snort3/snort3.git && cd snort3 ./configure_cmake.sh --prefix=/usr/local cd build && make -j"$(nproc)" && sudo make install snort -V snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -T The build is part of the audit Record how the binary was made: configure flags, DAQ version, whether Hyperscan was available. A sensor nobody can rebuild is a sensor nobody can trust after an incident — the same argument as verifying a package before installing it. 03 snort.lua is the product The configuration is a Lua table tree. Read it as documentation: every block names a stage of the pipeline and every value is a decision you can explain. -- /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua (the parts that matter) HOME_NET = '10.10.0.0/16' EXTERNAL_NET = '!$HOME_NET' ips = { enable_builtin_rules = false, rules = [[include /usr/local/etc/snort/rules/local.rules]], } stream = { memcap = 268435456 } stream_tcp = { policy = 'linux', session_timeout = 180 } alert_fast = { file = true, packet = false, limit = 10, } -- test the whole tree, and show every warning snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -T --warn-all HOME_NET from your asset list, never a guess: every $HOME_NET rule depends on it. One include per rule file you can name, so removing a rule set is one line, not an archaeology project. -T before every restart. A typo in Lua is a sensor that silently runs with defaults. 04 DAQ capture and threads DAQ is the layer between Snort and the kernel. afpacket is the workhorse on Linux; pcap is for portability and files; nfq is how inline works with iptables. # passive sensor on one interface sudo snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -i eth1 \ --daq afpacket --daq-var cluster_type=cluster_flow \ -A alert_fast -l /var/log/snort -q # see what the DAQ actually opened snort --daq-list snort --daq-dir /usr/local/lib/daq --daq-list # capture only what matters, at the kernel sudo snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -i eth1 -q \ --daq afpacket --daq-var 'bpf_file=/etc/snort/tap.bpf' # read a file instead of a wire snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -r capture.pcap -A alert_fast -k none -q Setting Meaning Common mistake cluster_flow One flow stays on one thread Using cluster_qm on a tap without RSS queues -k none Skip checksum validation Forgetting it on a NIC with offload, then blaming the rules snaplen Bytes kept per packet Truncating exactly the payload a rule needs BPF file Kernel-side filter Filtering out the traffic you later want to prove 05 Rule anatomy A Snort rule is a header that says who talks to whom, followed by options that say what the traffic must contain. Read it left to right and it is almost English. # action proto src sport -> dst dport (options) alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET 80 ( msg:"LAB web scanner user agent"; flow:to_server,established; content:"sqlmap"; http_header; classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000001; rev:1; ) Option What it constrains Notes flow Direction and connection state Needs stream enabled; without it, no match content Byte string in the payload Case-sensitive unless nocase http_header Buffer for the match Sticky buffer in Snort 3; replaces old uricontent tricks classtype Category and priority Drives triage; set it honestly sid Unique identity Local rules start at 1000000; never reuse a sid rev Revision of that sid Bump it when you change a rule, always For the semantics of the buffers and the full option list, use the official rule reference; for what a detection should say about an attack, the blue team page explains the loop around the rule. 06 Test rules against a pcap Never deploy a rule you have not seen fire and stay silent. Two runs — one against traffic that should match, one against traffic that must not — are the whole discipline. # 1. does the config still load? snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -T --warn-all # 2. does the rule fire on the malicious sample? snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua \ -R /usr/local/etc/snort/rules/local.rules \ -r samples/scan.pcap -A alert_fast -k none -q -l /tmp/snort-test cat /tmp/snort-test/alert_fast.txt # 3. does it stay quiet on normal traffic? snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua \ -R /usr/local/etc/snort/rules/local.rules \ -r samples/browsing.pcap -A alert_fast -k none -q -l /tmp/snort-clean wc -l /tmp/snort-clean/alert_fast.txt 2>/dev/null || echo "0 alerts: good" # 4. JSON for machines snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -r samples/scan.pcap -A alert_json -q \ -l /tmp/snort-json jq -r '.msg' /tmp/snort-json/alert_json.txt | sort | uniq -c A rule with no false-positive test is a rumour Keep both pcaps in the repository next to the rule. Six months later, the sample is the regression test that tells you a rule edit broke the detection — the same evidence habit as a checksum next to a binary. 07 Inline IPS and NFQUEUE Inline means Snort sees the packet before it is delivered, and can drop it. On Linux the least surprising way is nfq with iptables sending traffic to a queue. # send inbound traffic for the lab web server to queue 0 sudo iptables -I FORWARD -p tcp --dport 80 -j NFQUEUE --queue-num 0 # run Snort inline against that queue sudo snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -Q --daq nfq \ --daq-var queue=0 -A alert_fast -l /var/log/snort # in inline mode, drop is a real action drop tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 80 ( msg:"LAB blocked scanner"; flow:to_server,established; content:"sqlmap"; http_header; sid:1000002; rev:1; ) # prove the block, then prove the pass curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -A sqlmap http://10.10.11.10/ curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" http://10.10.11.10/ Decide what a crash means before it happens An inline sensor that dies is either a firewall that fails open or an outage that fails closed. Write the choice down, test it by stopping the service, and put the rule set behind a reviewed change. Start with one drop rule, not a downloaded feed of thirty thousand. 08 Snort 3 rule language changes Snort 2 habit Snort 3 replacement Why it matters uricontent content ...; http_uri; Sticky buffers instead of per-option prefix http_client_body option http_client_body buffer Same idea, new placement in the option list Preprocessor config Module blocks in snort.lua One language for config and rules alert_syslog only alert_fast , alert_json , alert_syslog Machine-readable output without a parser Unified2 consumers JSON alerts plus pcap logging Simpler pipeline, fewer broken parsers Migrated rule sets are the usual source of silent failure: a rule loads, warns about an unknown option, and never matches. -T --warn-all is how you hear that warning before production does. 09 Tuning before tuning policies Almost every "Snort drops packets" report is a capture or inspection budget problem, not a rule problem. Measure first: the interface counters, then Snort's own statistics. # kernel side: are we losing packets before Snort sees them? ip -s link show eth1 ethtool -S eth1 | grep -iE "drop|miss|error" # Snort side: which stage is expensive? sudo snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -i eth1 -q -A none \ --lua 'profiler = { modules = { show = true } }' # narrow the working set: HOME_NET, not the internet grep -n "HOME_NET" /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua Rule count is not the metric. Rule content is: a thousand cheap rules can cost less than fifty expensive ones. Turn off inspection you do not need — file carving, appid, full HTTP body on a tap that only needs headers. Match threads to queues, not to core count; a flow that hops threads loses state. Drop is a decision, silence is a metric. Record alert counts per day before and after every tuning change. 10 Hardening the sensor A sensor is a privileged process reading hostile bytes. Give it the two capabilities it needs and nothing else, and make sure the rest of the box cannot be edited by the account that Snort runs as. # /etc/systemd/system/snort.service [Unit] Description=Snort 3 IDS After=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=snort Group=snort ExecStartPre=/usr/local/bin/snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua -T ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/snort -c /usr/local/etc/snort/snort.lua \ -i eth1 --daq afpacket -A alert_fast -l /var/log/snort -q Restart=on-failure AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_ADMIN CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_ADMIN NoNewPrivileges=true ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=true PrivateTmp=true PrivateDevices=true ReadWritePaths=/var/log/snort RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_PACKET AF_INET AF_UNIX [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Every hardening line can blind the sensor After each change, confirm packets are still counted: restart, generate traffic, read one alert. A sandbox that silently denies AF_PACKET looks exactly like a quiet network. 11 Three proofs Proof Command Pass Config loads snort -c snort.lua -T --warn-all No error, no unknown-option warning Rule fires Replay the malicious pcap Exactly the expected sid, once Rule stays quiet Replay the benign pcap Zero alerts Inline blocks curl with the blocked header Connection dropped, alert logged Sensor keeps up ip -s link + Snort stats No kernel drops under normal load Keep the commands next to the config in the repository. For the same three proofs on the other engine, the Suricata manual is the mirror image; for the lab these sensors watch, see GNS3 . 12 Paranoid checklist HOME_NET matches the asset list, and nothing else. One local rule file, one sid range, one rev bump per edit. Every rule has a malicious pcap and a benign pcap beside it. -T --warn-all is part of the service start, not a habit. Inline mode has a documented fail-open or fail-closed decision, tested. Runs as an unprivileged user with two capabilities. Alert directory is writable, everything else is read-only. Log rotation and retention are configured before the disk fills. Rule set version and build flags recorded in one file. One alert per day reviewed manually — the sensor is not a dashboard. 13 Failure table Symptom Cause Fix Zero alerts on known-bad traffic Rule not included, or flow without stream Check the include path, then -T --warn-all Alerts on every packet Missing flow:to_server,established , or a bare content:"GET" Constrain direction, protocol and buffer Checksum errors fill the log NIC offload with the tap seeing pre-checksum frames -k none , or fix the offload Drops increase under load Threads vs queues, snaplen, or expensive rules Match cluster type, raise buffers, profile rules Inline mode passes everything No -Q , or iptables rule in the wrong chain Verify the NFQUEUE rule and the DAQ queue number Service runs, no traffic Hardening removed AF_PACKET or interface access Restore the capability, test with one packet Rule loads but never matches Snort 2 syntax on Snort 3 Rewrite with sticky buffers, re-test the pcap 14 Sources Snort — official documentation, rule reference and the DAQ guide. Suricata: Home Suricata / Sensor Signature engine · capture, rules, hardening Suricata: a sensor you can defend in an audit Anyone can install Suricata and see alerts. The hard part is a sensor that drops no packets , runs with the least privilege the kernel allows, and can prove in five minutes that it saw what it claims to have seen. This is the paranoid build: capture tuning, rule discipline, a hardened unit, and the checks that fail loudly when the sensor is lying. tested with -T, always AF_PACKET eve.json + PCAP non-root service 01 What a signature sensor can prove Suricata is three tools in one binary: an IDS (alerts on known patterns), an IPS (drops inline) and an NSM engine (protocol logs for DNS, HTTP, TLS, SMB and more). It is excellent at telling you a known pattern crossed the wire, and blind to intent. Mode What it means What you accept IDS (passive) Copies traffic from a tap or SPAN port Cannot block; must prove it saw everything IPS (inline) Traffic flows through the sensor Latency and outage risk if it fails open or closed NSM only Logs and metadata, minimal signature load Storage and privacy obligations The blind spot to state in writing Encrypted traffic hides intent. Suricata can log TLS SNI, certificates and JA3/JA4 fingerprints, but not the request inside. A sensor that claims to detect "data exfiltration" without TLS inspection is describing a hypothesis, not a control. Where this fits in a programme is the defenders page; the packet-level reading is tcpdump ; the Snort comparison is on the Snort page. 02 Install, and know what you installed Distro packages lag the upstream release, and features differ: Rust parsers, Hyperscan, AF_PACKET v3 and eBPF support are compile-time choices. Before trusting a rule, ask the binary what it was built with. sudo apt update sudo apt install -y suricata suricata-update jq suricata -V suricata --build-info | grep -Ei "AF_PACKET|LIBPCAP|HYPERSCAN|Rust|SIMD|NFQ" # configuration test: never restart without it sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml # what the running config actually resolved to sudo suricata --dump-config | grep -E "^(vars|af-packet|outputs)" | head -20 Pin the version you validated, whether that is a distro package or the OISF repository, and record it in the change log next to the rule set version. A sensor that updates itself silently is a sensor whose coverage you cannot describe. 03 Capture: interface, threads, offload Most "Suricata misses traffic" incidents are capture incidents. Choose the interface that sees the traffic you care about, give it enough ring buffer, and disable checksum validation when the NIC behind you offloads checksums — otherwise the sensor discards good packets as malformed. af-packet: - interface: eth1 cluster-id: 99 cluster-type: cluster_flow threads: 8 use-mmap: yes tpacket-v3: yes ring-size: 4096 block-size: 65536 bpf-filter: "not port 22" cluster_flow keeps a flow on one thread, which is what detection logic assumes; cluster_qm is faster but splits flows unless the NIC hashes correctly. threads should match receive queues, not cores. More threads than queues just adds locking. bpf-filter cuts noise before the engine sees it. Filter backup traffic, not the thing you are paid to detect. checksum-validation: no when the capture point receives offloaded frames; keep it on when the sensor is inline and can trust the wire. Confirm the NIC side as well: promiscuous mode on the sniff interface, a SPAN session that includes both directions, and enough MTU to see full frames. On a mirrored port, a missing direction is the classic silent half-blind sensor. 04 The config, block by block Keep suricata.yaml under version control and change it in small commits. The blocks that decide whether the sensor is honest are the network variables, the rule path and the outputs. vars: address-groups: HOME_NET: "[10.66.0.0/16,192.168.50.0/24]" EXTERNAL_NET: "!$HOME_NET" port-groups: HTTP_PORTS: "[80,8080]" SHELLCODE_PORTS: "!80" default-rule-path: /var/lib/suricata/rules rule-files: - suricata.rules - local.rules checksum-validation: no stream: memcap: 256mb reassembly: memcap: 128mb flow: memcap: 128mb HOME_NET is the single most consequential line in the file. Too broad and every internal scan is "external"; too narrow and direction-dependent rules never fire. Write it from the asset inventory, not from memory. 05 Rules: source, update, suppress A rule set is a dependency like any other: versioned, reviewed and tested. Use the maintained source, keep your own rules in a separate file, and document every suppression with a reason and a date. sudo suricata-update list-sources sudo suricata-update enable-source et/open sudo suricata-update sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml # your own rule, tested against a capture before it goes live cat >> /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules <<'RULE' alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"LAB union in query"; \ flow:to_server,established; http.uri; content:"union"; nocase; \ classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000001; rev:1;) RULE suricata -r ev/cap.pcap -S /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules -l ev/out jq -c 'select(.event_type=="alert") | {sig:.alert.signature, src:.src_ip, uri:.http.http_uri}' \ ev/out/eve.json Suppress by signature id and, where needed, by source, in threshold.config . A suppression without a ticket is a detection deleted by accident; log each one in the same repository as the rules. 06 Performance: MPM, memcaps, profile Tuning is a measurement exercise, not a config dump from a forum. Change one value, replay the same capture, compare the counters. Setting Effect When to touch it mpm-algo Pattern matcher: ac, ac-ks, hs, hs-ms Hyperscan builds: compare detection time on a fixed pcap detect.profile low / medium / high trade memory for speed Only after the drop counters are zero stream.memcap How much reassembly is buffered Long-lived sessions with big transfers rings/block-size Kernel-side buffering per thread Drops spike under bursty load The only performance signal that matters first is capture.kernel_drops . Everything else is optimisation on top of a sensor that may already be blind. 07 Hardening the service Suricata needs raw sockets, not root. Run it as a dedicated user with only the capabilities it needs, and let systemd enforce the rest. Apply one restriction per restart, and confirm the sensor still sees packets after each line. # /etc/systemd/system/suricata.service.d/10-paranoid.conf [Service] User=suricata Group=suricata NoNewPrivileges=yes ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=yes PrivateTmp=yes PrivateDevices=yes ProtectKernelTunables=yes ProtectKernelModules=yes ProtectControlGroups=yes RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX AF_PACKET CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_ADMIN AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_ADMIN RestrictSUIDSGID=yes LockPersonality=yes ReadWritePaths=/var/log/suricata /var/lib/suricata Hardening can blind a sensor PrivateDevices and a missing CAP_NET_RAW produce a service that starts, looks healthy, and captures nothing. After every line: systemctl restart suricata , wait one interval, then check capture.kernel_packets is still climbing. 08 Proving it works Three proofs, in order: the engine parses its config, a known-bad packet produces an alert, and the counters show no drops. Do all three after every change to config, rules or unit. # 1. config and rules parse sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml # 2. a capture with one known-bad request produces exactly one alert suricata -r ev/scan.pcap -S /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules -l ev/out jq -s 'map(select(.event_type=="alert")) | length' ev/out/eve.json # 3. the live sensor is not dropping and is still reading jq -c 'select(.event_type=="stats") | .stats.capture' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | tail -3 A replay is reproducible evidence; a live "looks fine" is an impression. Keep the pcap and the expected alert count next to the rule, so the next person can rerun it. 09 Operating: retention, integrity, triage The sensor writes evidence, so treat its disk as an evidence store: budget it, rotate it, and verify that nothing rewrote it. Retention is a contract question as much as a storage one. outputs: - eve-log: enabled: yes filetype: regular filename: eve.json community-id: true types: - alert - anomaly - dns - http - tls: {extended: yes} - flow - files - stats: {totals: yes, threads: no, interval: 60} - pcap-log: enabled: yes filename: pcap.log limit: 1gb max-files: 20 mode: normal Ship logs off the host within the retention window; a compromised sensor should not be the only copy. Hash the rule files after each update and keep the list with the change record. One time source. A sensor whose clock drifts produces a timeline you cannot use in an incident. Triage by signature class first , then by host: a single noisy rule can hide an entire campaign. Feed the alerts into the detection loop described on the defenders page, and keep the packet capture beside it: alerts say something happened, the pcap says what. 10 The paranoid checklist Check Pass condition Build known suricata --build-info recorded with the package version HOME_NET exact Matches the asset inventory, reviewed when a new subnet is added Both directions seen SPAN mirrors ingress and egress; a test flow appears twice No drops capture.kernel_drops stays at zero through a replay of peak traffic Config tested -T runs clean after every change, in CI if possible Rules reviewed Set version recorded; suppressions justified and dated Least privilege Service runs as suricata , no root, capabilities limited Proof retained A pcap plus expected alert count stored with each custom rule Logs leave the host Shipped within the retention window, stored read-only elsewhere Time synced Single NTP source, drift alerting enabled 11 Common failures Symptom Cause Fix Service runs, no packets Wrong interface, no promisc, or missing capability Check capture.kernel_packets , then the unit's capabilities Alerts stop after update Rule path or filename changed by the updater Verify default-rule-path and rule-files ; run -T Thousands of "checksum invalid" NIC offload at the capture point Set checksum-validation: no or disable offload on the tap Rules never fire HOME_NET wrong, or flow direction inverted Replay a pcap that should match and inspect flow events Drops under load Ring too small, too many threads, or CPU contention Increase ring-size / block-size , match threads to queues Sensor "healthy" but blind Hardening removed CAP_NET_RAW or hid the device Revert one line at a time; watch the counters No TLS content Encrypted by design Log SNI/JA3 and pair with endpoint telemetry 12 Sources Suricata — the official documentation, including the yaml reference. OISF — releases, the build matrix and the road map. ET — the open rule set most sensors start from. EVE — the JSON schema for every event type. update — the rule update tool and its sources. SELKS — a packaged sensor stack for comparison. For the defensive workflow around the sensor, read the defenders page; for the attack traffic it is meant to catch, the Kali manual. Defenders Attackers Snort Início Suricata / Sensor Motor de assinaturas · captura, regras, endurecimento Suricata: um sensor defensável numa auditoria Qualquer pessoa instala o Suricata e vê alertas. O difícil é um sensor que não perde pacotes , corre com o menor privilégio que o kernel permite e prova em cinco minutos que viu o que diz ter visto. Isto é a construção paranoica: afinação de captura, disciplina de regras, uma unit endurecida e as verificações que falham alto quando o sensor mente. sempre com -T AF_PACKET eve.json + PCAP serviço sem root 01 O que um sensor de assinaturas prova O Suricata são três ferramentas num binário: um IDS (alerta sobre padrões conhecidos), um IPS (descarta em linha) e um motor de NSM (registos de protocolo para DNS, HTTP, TLS, SMB e mais). É excelente a dizer que um padrão conhecido atravessou o fio, e cego quanto à intenção. Modo O que significa O que aceita IDS (passivo) Copía tráfego de um tap ou porta SPAN Não pode bloquear; tem de provar que viu tudo IPS (em linha) O tráfego atravessa o sensor Latência e risco de interrupção Só NSM Registos e metadados, carga mínima de assinaturas Armazenamento e obrigações de privacidade O ponto cego a escrever no relatório Tráfego cifrado esconde a intenção. O Suricata registra SNI, certificados e impressões JA3/JA4, não o pedido lá dentro. Um sensor que afirma detetar «exfiltração de dados» sem inspeção de TLS descreve uma hipótese, não um controlo. O lugar disto num programa está na página dos defensores ; a leitura ao nível do pacote está no tcpdump ; a comparação com o Snort está na página do Snort . 02 Instalar e saber o que se instalou Os pacotes da distribuição ficam atrás da versão upstream, e as funcionalidades diferem: parsers em Rust, Hyperscan, AF_PACKET v3 e eBPF são escolhas de compilação. Antes de confiar numa regra, pergunte ao binário com o que foi construído. sudo apt update sudo apt install -y suricata suricata-update jq suricata -V suricata --build-info | grep -Ei "AF_PACKET|LIBPCAP|HYPERSCAN|Rust|SIMD|NFQ" # teste de configuração: nunca reiniciar sem ele sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml # o que a configuração em execução realmente resolveu sudo suricata --dump-config | grep -E "^(vars|af-packet|outputs)" | head -20 Fixe a versão que validou, seja pacote da distribuição ou repositório da OISF, e registe-a no histórico de mudanças ao lado da versão do conjunto de regras. Um sensor que se atualiza em silêncio é um sensor cuja cobertura não consegue descrever. 03 Captura: interface, threads, offload A maioria dos incidentes de «o Suricata perde tráfego» são incidentes de captura. Escolha a interface que vê o tráfego que interessa, dê-lhe ring buffer suficiente e desative a validação de checksum quando a NIC atrás de si faz offload — caso contrário o sensor descarta pacotes bons como malformados. af-packet: - interface: eth1 cluster-id: 99 cluster-type: cluster_flow threads: 8 use-mmap: yes tpacket-v3: yes ring-size: 4096 block-size: 65536 bpf-filter: "not port 22" cluster_flow mantém um fluxo numa thread, que é o que a lógica de deteção assume; cluster_qm é mais rápido mas divide fluxos se a NIC não fizer o hash corretamente. threads deve acompanhar as filas de receção, não os núcleos. Mais threads que filas só acrescenta locks. bpf-filter corta ruído antes do motor o ver. Filtre tráfego de backup, não o que é pago para detetar. checksum-validation: no quando o ponto de captura recebe tramas com offload; mantenha ligado quando o sensor está em linha e pode confiar no fio. Confirme também o lado da NIC: modo promíscuo na interface de captura, uma sessão SPAN que inclua ambas as direções e MTU suficiente para ver tramas completas. Numa porta espelhada, uma direção em falta é o clássico sensor meio cego e silencioso. 04 O ficheiro de configuração, bloco a bloco Mantenha o suricata.yaml em controlo de versões e altere-o em commits pequenos. Os blocos que decidem se o sensor é honesto são as variáveis de rede, o caminho das regras e as saídas. vars: address-groups: HOME_NET: "[10.66.0.0/16,192.168.50.0/24]" EXTERNAL_NET: "!$HOME_NET" port-groups: HTTP_PORTS: "[80,8080]" SHELLCODE_PORTS: "!80" default-rule-path: /var/lib/suricata/rules rule-files: - suricata.rules - local.rules checksum-validation: no stream: memcap: 256mb reassembly: memcap: 128mb flow: memcap: 128mb HOME_NET é a linha de maior consequência do ficheiro. Demasiado ampla e cada varrimento interno é «externo»; demasiado estreita e regras dependentes de direção nunca disparam. Escreva-a a partir do inventário de ativos, não de memória. 05 Regras: fonte, atualização, supressão Um conjunto de regras é uma dependência como qualquer outra: versionada, revista e testada. Use a fonte mantida, guarde as suas regras num ficheiro separado e documente cada supressão com motivo e data. sudo suricata-update list-sources sudo suricata-update enable-source et/open sudo suricata-update sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml # regra própria, testada contra uma captura antes de ir para produção cat >> /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules <<'RULE' alert http $HOME_NET any -> $EXTERNAL_NET any (msg:"LAB union in query"; \ flow:to_server,established; http.uri; content:"union"; nocase; \ classtype:web-application-attack; sid:1000001; rev:1;) RULE suricata -r ev/cap.pcap -S /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules -l ev/out jq -c 'select(.event_type=="alert") | {sig:.alert.signature, src:.src_ip, uri:.http.http_uri}' \ ev/out/eve.json Suprima por identificador de assinatura e, quando necessário, por origem, no threshold.config . Uma supressão sem ticket é uma deteção apagada por acidente; registe cada uma no mesmo repositório das regras. 06 Desempenho: MPM, memcaps, perfil A afinação é um exercício de medição, não uma configuração copiada de um fórum. Mude um valor, repita a mesma captura, compare os contadores. Parâmetro Efeito Quando mexer mpm-algo Motor de padrões: ac, ac-ks, hs, hs-ms Compilações com Hyperscan: comparar tempo numa pcap fixa detect.profile low / medium / high trocam memória por velocidade Só depois de os contadores de perda estarem a zero stream.memcap Quanta reunião de fluxo é memorizada Sessões longas com grandes transferências rings/block-size Buffer do kernel por thread Perdas sob carga em rajada O único sinal de desempenho que importa primeiro é capture.kernel_drops . O resto é otimização em cima de um sensor que pode já estar cego. 07 Endurecer o serviço O Suricata precisa de raw sockets, não de root. Corra-o como utilizador dedicado, com apenas as capacidades necessárias, e deixe o systemd impor o resto. Aplique uma restrição por reinício e confirme que o sensor continua a ver pacotes depois de cada linha. # /etc/systemd/system/suricata.service.d/10-paranoid.conf [Service] User=suricata Group=suricata NoNewPrivileges=yes ProtectSystem=strict ProtectHome=yes PrivateTmp=yes PrivateDevices=yes ProtectKernelTunables=yes ProtectKernelModules=yes ProtectControlGroups=yes RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX AF_PACKET CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_ADMIN AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_RAW CAP_NET_ADMIN RestrictSUIDSGID=yes LockPersonality=yes ReadWritePaths=/var/log/suricata /var/lib/suricata O endurecimento pode cegar um sensor PrivateDevices e um CAP_NET_RAW em falta produzem um serviço que arranca, parece saudável e não captura nada. Depois de cada linha: systemctl restart suricata , espere um intervalo e confirme que capture.kernel_packets continua a subir. 08 Provar que funciona Três provas, por ordem: o motor interpreta a configuração, um pacote conhecidamente mau produz um alerta, e os contadores mostram ausência de perdas. Faça as três depois de cada alteração à configuração, às regras ou à unit. # 1. configuração e regras interpretam-se sudo suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml # 2. uma captura com um pedido mau produz exatamente um alerta suricata -r ev/scan.pcap -S /var/lib/suricata/rules/local.rules -l ev/out jq -s 'map(select(.event_type=="alert")) | length' ev/out/eve.json # 3. o sensor em produção não perde e continua a ler jq -c 'select(.event_type=="stats") | .stats.capture' /var/log/suricata/eve.json | tail -3 Uma repetição é evidência reproduzível; um «parece bem» ao vivo é uma impressão. Guarde a pcap e o número esperado de alertas ao lado da regra, para que a próxima pessoa possa repetir. 09 Operar: retenção, integridade, triagem O sensor escreve evidência, por isso trate o disco como um arquivo de evidência: dimensione-o, rode-o e verifique que ninguém o reescreveu. A retenção é uma questão de contrato tanto como de armazenamento. outputs: - eve-log: enabled: yes filetype: regular filename: eve.json community-id: true types: - alert - anomaly - dns - http - tls: {extended: yes} - flow - files - stats: {totals: yes, threads: no, interval: 60} - pcap-log: enabled: yes filename: pcap.

Stop using arrows and mouse clicks; start speaking Vim. The Grammar: [Count] + [Operator / Verb] + [Text Object / Motion] 01. Introduction & Modal Philosophy Traditional editors assume every key press inserts text. Vim assumes you spend most of your time reading, navigating, and refactoring code, reserving typing for specific modes. Normal Mode Esc / Ctrl+[ The command hub. Keys act as actions, navigation commands, and operators rather than text inputs. Insert Mode i / a / o Standard typing mode. Keypresses insert literal characters into the active buffer. Visual Mode v / V / Ctrl+v Highlight text regions character-wise ( v ), line-wise ( V ), or block-wise ( Ctrl+v ). Command-Line : / ? / ! Execute Ex commands for saving, quitting, buffer operations, search, and system execution. Select Mode gh Behaves like traditional IDE text highlighting where typing immediately overwrites selection. Terminal Mode :terminal Interacts with an embedded terminal shell directly inside a Vim window split. 02. Basic Navigation & Fundamental Editing Master home-row navigation and fundamental editing mechanics before learning complex sequences. Category Keys Action Description Core Directional h j k l Left, Down, Up, Right (keep hands on home-row) Word Motions w / W | b / B Next word / WORD start | Previous word / WORD start Word Endings e / E | ge / gE Forward to end of word / WORD | Backward to end of word / WORD Line Bounds 0 | ^ | $ Column 0 (absolute start) | First non-whitespace char | End of line Inline Character Find f{char} / t{char} Find character forward / Till character forward (place cursor before) Repeat Find ; / , Repeat last f/t search forward / Repeat backward Vertical Paging Ctrl+u / Ctrl+d Scroll half-page Up / Scroll half-page Down File Navigation gg / G | {num}G First line of buffer / Last line of buffer | Jump directly to line {num} The Dot Operator (.) The single most powerful core command in Vim. . repeats the last editing change (e.g., cw + type word + Esc , then hit . on another word to instantly replace it). 03. Text Objects & Advanced Motions Text objects allow operating on structural constructs (words, quotes, brackets, tags) regardless of where the cursor is inside the object. Inner ( i ) vs Around ( a ) i targets only the content inside the boundaries. a targets the content PLUS surrounding delimiters & whitespace . Common Target Objects w / s / p - Words, Sentences, Paragraphs " , ' , ` - Single, Double, or Backtick Quotes ( , [ , { , < - Parentheses, Brackets, Braces, Angle brackets t - HTML / XML Tags Expression Command Target Text Resulting Action ciw const variable = true; Deletes inner word and drops into Insert mode. di" console.log(" Hello World "); Wipes text inside quotes, keeping empty quotes "" . da( func (arg1, arg2) ; Deletes parentheses AND everything contained inside. cit

Changes contents between opening and closing HTML tags. 04. Registers, Marks & Macros Store text snippets, bookmark arbitrary code lines, and record repetitive keystroke sequences for massive automation. OdicforceSounds Em Português Doze capítulos Dossiê · Índice ◉ Como usar este índice Nove páginas deste arquivo tratam da mesma coisa por ângulos diferentes: a força que guarda a lei, o papel que a autoriza e o número que raramente aparece. Este documento não repete nenhuma delas — liga-as, explica o método que todas partilham e diz o que ainda falta escrever. A regra é simples: uma página, uma pergunta . Os dossiês sobre a PSP, a GNR e a Polícia Judiciária respondem «quem é esta força e o que faz»; os dossiês sobre anonimato e ordem pública respondem «porque é que a farda esconde quem age»; os manuais respondem «como se lê a prova» e «o que se pode exigir». Nenhum deles é uma acusação colectiva, e todos declaram os seus limites antes de concluir. Nota de método Nada aqui é denúncia individual. Não há nomes, coordenadas, horários, efetivos operacionais nem material sensível. O que se publica é aquilo que já é público — relatórios, comunicados, sentenças, estatísticas — e o que se pede é sempre o mesmo: que o número exista, que seja comparável e que alguém responda por ele. ▤ A anatomia de um dossiê As três peças centrais — A Força Pública e o Tigre Oculto , GNR — O Dragão que Guarda a Lei e A Serpente e o Macaco — seguem a mesma ordem. Não é acaso: é o que permite compará-las. O esqueleto comum dos três dossiês Passo O que faz Porque importa 01 O símbolo O tigre, o dragão, a serpente. Um brasão diz o que a instituição quer ser; a história diz o que ela foi. 02 A origem Datas e modelos estrangeiros. Uma força criada para ser respeitada comporta-se de forma diferente de uma criada para ser querida. 03 O mapa Divisões, comandos, unidades. Sem mapa, qualquer crítica é sobre «a polícia» em geral — ou seja, sobre nada. 04 Os números Efetivo, ocorrências, queixas, tempos. O passo onde a maioria dos dossiês morre, porque os dados não existem ou não são comparáveis. 05 Os casos Episódios lidos como sintomas, não como troféus. Um caso isolado não prova um sistema; cinco casos com o mesmo desfecho começam a provar. 06 O que funciona A parte que quase ninguém escreve: o que a força faz bem. Sem ela, o dossiê é propaganda ao contrário. 07 As sombras Cada falha com um comentário educativo — não com um insulto. 08 Seis medidas Cada uma com forma de medir. Uma proposta sem indicador é uma opinião. 09 Fontes Relatórios, comunicados, dados de outubro de 2026. Verificáveis, datados, citáveis. O passo 08 é o que distingue este conjunto de tudo o resto: uma medida só entra se vier acompanhada do número que a pode desmentir. «Mais formação» não é medida; «horas de formação em uso da força por agente, publicadas anualmente» é. ⚖ As três forças, em números e em papel Portugal tem três corpos com mandatos que se tocam e não se substituem: uma força urbana, uma força territorial militarizada e uma polícia de investigação criminal dirigida pelo processo. Quem faz o quê, e desde quando Força Nascimento Território Mandato Dossiê PSP Polícia de Segurança Pública 1832, como Guarda Nacional Cidades — sobretudo Lisboa e Porto Ordem pública, policiamento de proximidade, contra-ordenações O Tigre Oculto GNR Guarda Nacional Republicana 1801, como Guarda Real; 1911 na forma republicana Interior, estradas, litoral Policiamento territorial, trânsito, fiscalidade, protecção civil O Dragão que Guarda a Lei PJ Polícia Judiciária Polícia do juiz, na tradição do processo Nacional, por competência Investigação criminal, prova, perícia A Serpente e o Macaco A distinção entre a PSP e a GNR não é apenas geográfica — é de ritmo e de pressão. Uma polícia de cidade vive o chão, o metro e a noite; uma guarda territorial vive a estrada, a aldeia, o incêndio e a fronteira. A PJ é outra coisa: entra depois do crime e antes do tribunal, e a sua força é o processo, não o bastão. Todos Repare no que a cronologia mostra sem comentário: entre o anúncio e a entrega passam três anos, e o indicador mais eloquente de capacidade administrativa não é a promessa — é a data em que o concurso sai. ◍ O anonimato como tecnologia A farda que ninguém consegue identificar defende uma tese simples e difícil de refutar: o anonimato não é um detalhe do uniforme, é o mecanismo que produz a impunidade. A página compara os dois laboratórios onde a letalidade policial foi medida — Brasil e Estados Unidos — e depois o país onde quase ninguém morre e quase ninguém é responsabilizado. O contraste é o argumento: onde a morte é rara, a ausência de responsabilização continua a ser a norma, e isso só se explica se o problema não for a violência mas a identificação. O uniforme não é um álibi continua a análise no terreno da ordem pública e da habitação, e distingue dois anonimatos : o de quem manifesta — que é um direito — e o de quem carrega o bastão — que é uma escolha institucional. Confundir os dois é o erro que a página desmonta. A frase que resolve a discussão «Apenas cumpria ordens» não é uma defesa. É uma confissão: confessa que a ordem existia, que foi cumprida e que ninguém, em nenhum ponto da cadeia, a julgou. Uma instituição que só sabe obedecer não pode invocar discricionariedade quando lhe convém. ▦ Os números — e o que eles não dizem Police Victims & Officers Victimized é a revisão de dados do conjunto: vítimas civis e agentes vitimados, lado a lado, com fontes. Não há tempo médio de resposta por comando, número de queixas contra agentes com o respectivo desfecho, ocorrências de uso da força, nem percentagem de casos que chegam a tribunal. É o único documento do conjunto que oferece uma régua em vez de uma conclusão: o leitor calcula o seu próprio engulo — quanto do seu mês vai para o sonho de outra pessoa — e compara. A parte sobre a justiça a favor do regime não é uma teoria: está no Livro também, e a página cita-o. Uma casa não é um prémio por bom comportamento. É a condição sem a qual não há comportamento para premiar. ✓ Quatro filtros e sete dias Armas Não São Conteúdo é o manual de discrição institucional do conjunto — e o mais imediatamente aplicável. Parte de uma frase que serve de regra: uma fotografia é um mapa, não um troféu. Os quatro filtros, antes de publicar ou de mostrar Filtro Pergunta Se falhar Necessidade Alguém precisa de ver isto para exercer um direito? Não publicar Proporção O detalhe mostrado é proporcional ao que se quer demonstrar? Reduzir ao mínimo Consentimento Quem aparece escolheu aparecer? SDK levels are not version numbers Three integers look similar and mean completely different things. Getting them confused produces apps that either crash on old phones or get rejected by Play. minSdk — the oldest Android version that may install the app. Set by device reach and library requirements. A low value costs testing surface; a high value costs users. compileSdk — the platform JAR your code compiles against. Newer APIs need a newer value. It does not change runtime behavior. targetSdk — the behavior contract at runtime. It decides whether Android applies new restrictions (background limits, notification permission, photo picker behavior). Raising it is a migration, not a checkbox. A real project shape for 2026: minSdk 26 (covers devices that still receive security updates and meets most modern library floors), compileSdk 37 , targetSdk 36 while you test 37's behavior changes. It is to move the project forward one axis at a time: Gradle wrapper first, then AGP, then Kotlin and the Compose compiler, then compileSdk , then targetSdk .
